summary:
On low ground under trees, NISAR flagged 17 km² (95% interval 15 to 19 km²) more flooding than in the 12 days before, where Sentinel-1 saw dry land (evidence, not verified).

On open water: F1 0.05 for NISAR and 0.17 for Sentinel-1, checked against optical satellites. The difference, NISAR minus Sentinel-1, is −0.12 (95% interval −0.20 to −0.03), below our non-inferiority margin of −0.05. Recall was low for every radar map, OPERA's own Sentinel-1 product included, most likely because the optical check had no clear pre-flood image and counted water that was already standing.

On 27 Sep 2026 the Gandak river in Bihar broke its flood record, and NASA-ISRO's new NISAR radar imaged it the next day, with Europe's Sentinel-1 11 hours later. Today's global radar flood maps use Sentinel-1's short C-band waves, which bounce off leaves, so water under trees often goes unmapped; NISAR's longer L-band waves reach the ground underneath. Our app lets anyone watch the flood spread every 12 days, slide between the two radars' flood maps, tap a field and hear its radar signal change, and see how we checked it.
details:
What it does
Dancing with the SARS is a one-page web app that shows exactly what flood maps miss under trees. We took the record-breaking Gandak River flood in Bihar (27 Sep 2026), where NASA-ISRO's new NISAR (L-band) and Europe's Sentinel-1 (C-band) passed over just 11 hours apart. The app has five simple steps: watch the river spread every 12 days, slide between the two radars' flood maps, see the "hidden steps" (where NISAR found water under trees that Sentinel-1 missed), tap the map to hear a field's radar signal change, and see exactly how we checked our math. It runs entirely on GitHub Pages, works on a phone, and needs no login.

How we made the maps
We used seven NISAR L2 GCOV dates (provisional, HH and HV on track 149), averaged to a 40-meter grid. To make sure we were only looking at real data, we removed pixels that weren't fully focused or had slopes over 10 degrees, and we corrected for calibration offsets by measuring stable ground (high ground and raised towns). For our water thresholds, we used a per-tile bimodality test (Ashman D > 2) with Kittler-Illingworth thresholding on 10 km tiles. New open water is an HH drop of at least 3 dB below that threshold (with HV also dark). Flooded vegetation is an HH rise of at least 3 dB that beats the HV change by 2 dB (a double-bounce off tree trunks). We locked in every single threshold before the event started—we didn't want to tune the math after seeing the results.

How we checked it (and what we found)
We validated our maps against optical satellites (Landsat 9 and Sentinel-2C).

  • Under trees (Claim 2): On low ground under trees where Sentinel-1 saw dry land, NISAR flagged 17 km² more flooding (95% interval 15 to 19 km²) than the 12 days prior. We noted that 52% of these pixels sit near buildings (walls can cause fake double-bounces), so we proudly label this layer "evidence, not verified." On cropland, the signal disappeared entirely (−105 km²).
  • Open water (Claim 1): Sentinel-1 actually beat NISAR on open water (F1 of 0.17 vs 0.05), failing our pre-set non-inferiority margin. But we dug into why: recall was low for every radar map (even OPERA's official one), because 90% of the water we "missed" was already dark on Sep 16. Without a clear pre-flood optical image, the optical referee was likely counting standing water that our change detector correctly ignored.
  • NISAR alone (Claim 1a): Checked against the Sep 29 Sentinel-2B map in the western frame, NISAR's F1 jumped to 0.68 (95% interval 0.53 to 0.76).

What this can't tell you
Because no satellite can see through a canopy, this is evidence of water, not a perfect accuracy figure. It won't tell you about structural damage, it's only one flood in Bihar, and the NISAR data is PROVISIONAL (the final validated reprocessing is due by the end of 2026). Also, NISAR's 12-day revisit means this is for post-flood verification (data arrives 36–72 hours later), not first response.

Tools
Python (numpy, scipy, h5py, rasterio, GDAL, scikit-learn, matplotlib), MapLibre GL JS, PMTiles, the Web Audio API, Playwright and FFmpeg for the video, and GitHub Pages.

NASA data
NISAR L2 GCOV PROVISIONAL (ASF DAAC), OPERA L3 DSWx-S1 v1 (PO.DAAC), OPERA L3 DSWx-HLS v1 (PO.DAAC), and OPERA L2 RTC-S1 v1 (ASF DAAC).

Other data and tools
ESA WorldCover 2021 v200, JRC Global Surface Water occurrence v1.4, Copernicus GLO-30 DEM and HAND, and GHSL GHS-BUILT-S E2020 R2023A.

AI use
The team used an AI coding assistant to accelerate development. Its role was limited to UI scaffolding, writing test harnesses, and debugging the pipeline. The team designed and authored all scientific logic, including the thresholding, the bimodality gate, and the optical-reference validation. No generative image, video, or audio model was used; the two diagrams are SVG drawings coded from basic shapes and marked "Diagram made with AI assistance."
